# Ronnie O'Sullivan Profile: World Titles and Records
Explore Ronnie O'Sullivan's journey from prodigious snooker talent to record-breaking world champion and an icon of the sport.
Published: 5 August 2026, 18:24 UTC • Updated: 24 August 2026, 13:45 UTC • [Billy Reid](https://worldinsport.com/author/billyreid124/) • 12 mins read • [ 0 ](https://worldinsport.com/ronnie-osullivan-profile-career-records/#respond)

Ronnie O’Sullivan’s career is traced from prodigious junior success to record-breaking longevity at the top of snooker. The profile covers his seven World Championships, 41 ranking titles and 23 Triple Crown wins, along with his fast, precise style and the influence of his technical and mental development.
It also examines setbacks, including personal struggles, withdrawals and uneven spells, showing how he remained a major force across different eras. His records, scoring landmarks and lasting impact on the sport place him among the key figures in snooker history.
Ronnie O’Sullivan has spent more than three decades making elite snooker appear deceptively simple. The speed of his decision-making, the precision of his positional play and the fluency of his break-building have given him a style unlike anyone else’s. However, natural ability alone does not explain his career.
Seven World Championships, a record 41 ranking titles and an unmatched 23 Triple Crown victories show how often O’Sullivan has converted that ability into results. He has won major tournaments as a teenager, an established champion and a veteran, while competing against several generations of leading players.
That longevity places him at the centre of any discussion about snooker’s greatest player. Stephen Hendry matched his seven world titles in the Crucible era, Steve Davis shaped the sport’s television boom and John Higgins built an exceptional all-round record. O’Sullivan’s case rests on the combination of major honours, scoring records, technical range and lasting public appeal.
This Ronnie O’Sullivan profile examines how an unusually gifted junior became the defining player of modern snooker, without overlooking the setbacks. And personal struggles that made his career far less straightforward than his cue action sometimes suggested.
[Embed from Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/2272396220)
## Early Life and Exceptional Junior Development
Ronald Antonio O’Sullivan was born on 5 December 1975 in Wolverhampton, West Midlands, before growing up in Chigwell, Essex. His father encouraged his interest in snooker, and the family installed a full-sized table at home, allowing him to develop through long and focused practice sessions.
His ability became apparent almost immediately. O’Sullivan compiled a break of 117 at the age of 10 and won the British Under-16 Championship when he was 13. At 15, he made a competitive maximum break at the 1991 English Amateur Championship. He then won the World Under-21 Championship in India before turning professional in 1992.
The transition to the professional circuit was remarkably quick. O’Sullivan won 74 of his first 76 qualifying matches, including 38 in succession. Those results showed that his reputation was not based only on eye-catching practice performances. He could reproduce his scoring power under competitive pressure.
His family circumstances changed dramatically at the same time. O’Sullivan’s father received a life sentence in 1992, when his son was 16. O’Sullivan has since spoken publicly about the pressure and disruption surrounding that period, which coincided with the beginning of his professional career.
## A Teenage Breakthrough at the UK Championship
O’Sullivan’s breakthrough arrived at the 1993 UK Championship. Still only 17, he defeated Steve Davis and Stephen Hendry on his way to the title, becoming the youngest winner of a ranking tournament.
The significance went beyond the age record. Davis had been the dominant player of the previous decade, while Hendry was establishing his own period of control. Beating both during the same tournament demonstrated that O’Sullivan could already compete with the sport’s leading champions.
Just over a year later, he defeated Higgins to win the 1995 Masters at the age of 19. He remains the youngest champion in the tournament’s history. His rapid play and attacking shot selection also made him one of snooker’s most recognisable competitors before he had reached his twenties.
The nickname “The Rocket” reflected his pace, but speed was never the whole explanation. O’Sullivan played quickly because he read patterns early. He often identified the route through a break before completing its opening shots, allowing him to move around the table with little visible hesitation.
## The Maximum Break That Defined His Style
The clearest early expression of O’Sullivan’s approach came at the 1997 World Championship. Facing Mick Price at the Crucible Theatre, he completed a 147 in five minutes and eight seconds.
It remains the fastest officially recognised maximum break in professional competition. O’Sullivan averaged less than nine seconds for each shot, including the time required for the referee to replace the colours.
The achievement is sometimes reduced to speed, but its technical quality was equally important. O’Sullivan controlled the cue ball so precisely that he rarely needed to pause or recover from poor position. The break looked spontaneous because the preparation for each shot had already taken place in his mind.
World in Sport’s guide to [what makes a maximum break so difficult](https://worldinsport.com/maximum-break-what-it-really-takes/ "Maximum Break: What It Really Takes to Make Snooker History") provides further context for the positional control and concentration required to complete all 36 pots.
## Turning Talent into World Titles
Despite his early success, the World Championship proved difficult to master at first. O’Sullivan lost in the semi-finals three times between 1996 and 1999, leaving questions about whether his attacking game could withstand the longer matches and tactical demands of the Crucible.
He answered them in 2001. O’Sullivan defeated Higgins 18-14 in the final to secure his first world title, eight years after becoming a ranking-event champion. The victory helped him reach world number one for the first time during the following season.
A second world crown followed in 2004, when he overwhelmed Graeme Dott 18-8. Six-time world champion Ray Reardon had become an important mentor, encouraging greater patience and helping O’Sullivan strengthen the tactical side of his game.
The partnership mattered because it challenged the assumption that O’Sullivan relied entirely on instinct. His scoring was already exceptional, but Reardon helped him become harder to break down during poor spells. 
World in Sport’s [profile of Ray Reardon](https://worldinsport.com/ray-reardon-the-snooker-legend-who-changed-the-game/ "Ray Reardon: The Snooker Legend Who Changed the Game") explores the former champion’s influence on O’Sullivan’s development.
O’Sullivan won his third world title in 2008, again completing an 18-8 victory, this time against Ali Carter. By then, he had become a more complete competitor. He could still overwhelm opponents with scoring bursts, but he was also more willing to win slow frames through safety play and disciplined shot selection.
## Personal Struggles and an Uneasy Relationship with Snooker
O’Sullivan’s career has never followed a smooth path. He has spoken openly about depression, problems with alcohol and drugs earlier in his life, and the psychological strain he associated with professional competition.
His openness has added important context to periods of inconsistency, tournament withdrawals and repeated suggestions that he might retire. It does not excuse every controversial incident or public disagreement, but it helps explain why his relationship with snooker has often appeared conflicted.
Running became an important source of structure away from the table. He also worked with psychiatrist Steve Peters, whose methods helped him manage pressure and respond more calmly to mistakes during matches.
The effect became particularly visible during the early 2010s. Rather than attempting to eliminate every negative thought, O’Sullivan became better at preventing frustration from controlling the next shot or frame. That mental adjustment complemented the technical maturity he had developed with Reardon.
## The 2012 and 2013 Crucible Triumphs
O’Sullivan defeated Carter 18-11 in the 2012 World Championship final to claim his fourth title. He then stepped away from almost the entire following season, playing only one competitive match before returning to Sheffield as defending champion.
His successful defence in 2013 remains one of the defining achievements of his career. With little competitive preparation, he beat Barry Hawkins 18-12 in the final and became the first player since Hendry in 1996 to retain the world title.
The performance demonstrated that O’Sullivan’s game depended on more than rhythm gained through constant tournament play. His basic technique, knowledge of the table and ability to manage long matches remained intact despite the extended absence.
He came close to winning a third consecutive title in 2014, but Mark Selby recovered to beat him 18-14 in the final. Selby’s ability to slow the contest, create complicated tactical exchanges and punish errors exposed a continuing challenge: O’Sullivan was at his most dangerous when dictating the rhythm. But opponents who disrupted that rhythm could make him uncomfortable.
## A Playing Style Built on Control, Not Only Speed
O’Sullivan is generally described as snooker’s most naturally gifted player, although that description can understate the work behind his technique.
His greatest strength is cue-ball control. He regularly leaves straightforward positional routes that reduce the difficulty of the next pot. That control allows him to compile large breaks without repeatedly relying on recovery shots.
His cue action is compact and repeatable, with little unnecessary movement. He can also compete to a high standard with either hand, switching to his left rather than using the rest for certain shots. That ability changes the angles available to him and helps maintain the flow of a break.
O’Sullivan is also an exceptional front-runner. Once an opponent makes a mistake, he can remove the remaining reds and settle a frame in one visit. The speed of that punishment places additional pressure on opponents because a single loose safety shot may cost them the frame.
However, his best World Championship performances have depended equally on patience. Later in his career, he became more selective about ambitious pots and more comfortable leaving the cue ball safe when an attack carried unnecessary risk.
## Ronnie O’Sullivan’s Major Titles and Records
The following figures are correct to 5 August 2026 and may change while O’Sullivan remains active. 
They are based on the [official WPBSA player record](https://www.wpbsa.com/player/ronnie-osullivan/).   
| Achievement  | Total  | Career context  |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| World Championship titles  | 7  | Won in 2001, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, 2020 and 2022  |  
| UK Championship titles  | 8  | Competition record  |  
| Masters titles  | 8  | Competition record  |  
| Triple Crown titles  | 23  | All-time record  |  
| Ranking-event titles  | 41  | All-time record  |  
| Ratified maximum breaks  | 17  | All-time professional record  |  
| Highest professional break  | 153  | Set at the 2026 World Open  |  
O’Sullivan reached another scoring landmark at the 2019 Players Championship, becoming the first professional to compile 1,000 career century breaks. The moment was especially fitting because the century completed his victory over Neil Robertson in the final.
His records at the UK Championship and Masters also illustrate the unusual span of his career. O’Sullivan is both the youngest and oldest winner of each event. He secured his eighth UK title in December 2023 and his eighth Masters crown the following month, beating Ding Junhui and Carter respectively.
## Matching Hendry at the Crucible
O’Sullivan’s sixth world title arrived in 2020 after a seven-year wait. He defeated Kyren Wilson 18-8 and moved beyond Hendry’s record of 36 ranking-event victories.
Two years later, he beat Judd Trump 18-13 in the 2022 final to secure a seventh world championship. At 46, he became the oldest Crucible champion, surpassing the age record previously held by Reardon.
The victory drew him level with Hendry’s modern-era total of seven world titles. The comparison between them remains subjective. Hendry’s dominance during the 1990s was more complete, while O’Sullivan’s success has extended over a much longer period and across a deeper international tour.
For an explanation of the tournament’s long-match structure and why it presents a different challenge from other events, read World in Sport’s guide to the [World Snooker Championship format](https://worldinsport.com/world-snooker-championship-format-explained/ "How Does the World Snooker Championship Format Work?").
## New Records at the Age of 50
O’Sullivan continued to produce unprecedented scoring achievements late in his career. At the 2025 Saudi Arabia Masters, he made two 147s during the same one-session match against Chris Wakelin.
They were the 16th and 17th ratified maximums of his professional career. He became the first player to make two maximum breaks on the same day and the oldest player to record an official competitive 147.
In March 2026, O’Sullivan compiled a break of 153 against Ryan Day at the World Open. A free ball effectively provided a 16th red, allowing him to surpass Jamie Burnett’s previous professional high of 148.
The [World Snooker Tour account of the 153 break](https://www.wst.tv/news/2026/march/20/o-sullivan-makes-snooker-s-highest-ever-break-with-historic-153-1/) confirmed it as the highest break in professional snooker history. It was another example of O’Sullivan adding to his records long after most players would have entered a purely ceremonial stage of their career.
[Embed from Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/2272571235)
## The Later-Career Challenge
Late-career O’Sullivan remains capable of elite performances, although his schedule and form have become less predictable. Medical withdrawals and extended periods away from tournament play have interrupted his momentum, while younger opponents have reduced the margin for error.
He reached the 2026 World Open final before losing 10-7 to Thepchaiya Un-Nooh. At the World Championship, O’Sullivan led Higgins 9-4 in their second-round match but lost 13-12 after a major comeback from his long-time rival.
He returned to the Crucible shortly afterwards and won the 2026 World Seniors Championship on his debut, defeating Joe Perry 10-4 in the final. O’Sullivan said after the event that his confidence had been low, but that he wanted to enjoy attacking snooker and finish his career strongly.
That result did not carry ranking points or the competitive depth of a main-tour world title. Nevertheless, it showed that the desire to perform had not disappeared. As of the statistical cut-off, O’Sullivan remained an active professional and was listed 14th in the world rankings.
## Influence on Snooker and Its Audience
O’Sullivan’s wider importance is not based solely on trophies. His style made break-building accessible to viewers who might not otherwise follow the tactical details of snooker.
Like Jimmy White before him, he brought speed, unpredictability and visible personality to a sport often associated with restraint. 
World in Sport’s [Jimmy White profile](https://worldinsport.com/jimmy-white-profile-snooker-whirlwind-records/ "Jimmy White Profile: The Whirlwind Who Made Snooker Feel Alive") explains how White helped establish the appetite for attacking, emotionally engaging players before O’Sullivan’s arrival.
O’Sullivan then combined that appeal with a record of sustained major success. His matches have remained central to tournament promotion, particularly in Britain and China, while his willingness to discuss pressure has remained central. And mental health has revealed the strain behind an individual sport in which players spend long periods isolated at the table.
He has also influenced how attacking players are assessed. Speed alone is no longer enough. The standard associated with O’Sullivan includes rapid pattern recognition, precise cue-ball control and the ability to turn a small opening into a frame-winning contribution.
Readers can find further career features covering influential athletes from across sport in World in Sport’s [sports profile collection](https://worldinsport.com/category/sports-profiles/).
## Ronnie O’Sullivan’s Place in Snooker History
No single statistic settles the debate about snooker’s greatest player. Hendry’s seven world titles came during a period of extraordinary dominance. Davis helped transform the professional game, while Higgins has matched scoring ability with tactical excellence across a similarly long career.
O’Sullivan’s claim is built on range. He owns the ranking-title and Triple Crown records, shares the modern World Championship record and has compiled more centuries and ratified maximums than anyone else. He has also remained capable of setting new scoring records at 50.
His career has included absences, uneven form, disciplinary issues and a complicated relationship with the sport. Those elements prevent the story from becoming a straightforward celebration. They also make his longevity more significant. O’Sullivan repeatedly returned from difficult periods and found new ways to compete.
The most accurate assessment is not that everything came easily to him. Some individual shots may have looked effortless, but maintaining a place among the world’s best for more than three decades required adaptation, resilience and technical discipline.
That combination explains why Ronnie O’Sullivan matters. He did not merely collect the strongest statistical record of the modern era. He changed the pace, expectations and public image of professional snooker while building a career whose full span may prove as difficult to match as any single record.
